mcqs.question: Why do attackers so often prefer social engineering over exploiting a technical vulnerability?
options: Social engineering is illegal in fewer jurisdictions than hacking
Firewalls cannot detect any form of email traffic
Most companies have no email filtering at all
It exploits consistent psychological levers — authority, urgency, fear, helpfulness — that are far cheaper to trigger than breaking a hardened, patched system
mcqs.explanation: Breaking modern cryptography or a patched, hardened server takes real skill and time; getting one person to click a well-crafted email exploits universal human defaults and takes far less effort. The other options aren't the actual reason attackers gravitate here.

mcqs.question: A phishing email has perfect grammar, a plausible sender, and a convincing pretext. What defense actually scales against this, given that "spot the bad grammar" no longer works?
options: Verifying the sender or the request through a second, independent channel before acting
Only opening email on a mobile device instead of a desktop
Relying on the recipient's general intelligence to notice something is off
Assuming any email with a real company logo is legitimate
mcqs.explanation: Modern phishing is often grammatically flawless and visually convincing, so recognition-based defenses degrade. Verifying through a second channel — calling a known number, checking with the purported sender directly — doesn't depend on spotting a tell, which is why it generalizes across even well-crafted attempts.

mcqs.question: Why have attackers increasingly shifted toward vishing and smishing rather than relying purely on email phishing?
options: Phone and SMS channels bypass many of the spam filters and link-scanning tools now common on email, and people apply less scrutiny to them
Email phishing has become technically impossible due to encryption
Phone calls and texts are free to send in unlimited volume, unlike email
SMS messages cannot legally be blocked by carriers
mcqs.explanation: As email defenses improved, attackers moved to channels with weaker automated filtering and where recipients tend to be less guarded — the psychology (urgency, authority) stays the same, only the channel changes to dodge the newer email-side controls.

mcqs.question: Why is business email compromise (BEC) hard for automated email security tools to catch, compared to a phishing email with a malicious link?
options: A BEC email is typically just plausible-looking text requesting a routine action, with no malicious link or attachment for a filter to flag
BEC emails are always sent from a domain that's on every known blocklist
BEC always involves a virus attachment that antivirus tools should catch but don't
BEC only targets email providers that don't support spam filtering
mcqs.explanation: BEC's entire payload is a well-timed, well-researched request in ordinary text — no exploit, no link, no attachment — so there's nothing for signature- or link-based filtering to flag. That's exactly why the effective control is procedural (out-of-band verification), not technical scanning.

mcqs.question: In a phishing attack chain (email sent → link clicked → credentials entered on a fake page → attacker logs in → lateral movement), which single control breaks the chain even after the credential has already been stolen?
options: MFA on the account, since a correct password alone is no longer sufficient to log in
Better email filtering, since the email has already been delivered by this point
Awareness training, since the user has already made the click decision
Encrypting the fake login page's traffic
mcqs.explanation: By the time the credential is harvested, filtering and training have already had their chance and missed — MFA is the control that still works downstream of that failure, because a stolen password alone can't complete a login without the second factor.

mcqs.question: A security team argues that phishing simulations and mandatory MFA don't need to apply to their own security engineers, since they'd "obviously never fall for it." What does the RSA 2011 breach suggest about that reasoning?
options: It suggests technical staff are only vulnerable to smishing, not email phishing
It suggests that a well-researched, well-timed spear-phishing attempt succeeded against a security-focused company, showing technical knowledge reduces but doesn't eliminate susceptibility
It suggests MFA would not have helped RSA regardless of the breach's cause
It suggests the breach was unrelated to social engineering
mcqs.explanation: RSA's breach began with a spear-phishing email opened by an employee at a company whose entire business was security — clear evidence that expertise lowers but doesn't remove risk. Controls need to apply uniformly rather than carve out an exception for people who feel confident they're immune.
